a:
This calendar is the graduate dissertation of an expert in Homo sapiens culture and society. 

Homo sapiens was a species of literate primate on the planet Sol-3.

Because this species lived so long ago, and so far away, we have to make some educated guesses about their traditions based on the few facts we know for certain.

Fortunately, we have strong evidence that humans shared Sol-3 with at least 10,928 bird species.

And we know that they used a calendar of 365 days and 12 months.

It stands to reason that they would designate specific days to celebrate each bird species.

Competing theories about a "Calendar of Mammals" are not to be trusted!

q: Why is January the month of waterfowl?
a:
With the new year, January was a time of renewal, symbolized in human society by the transformation of an unsightly duckling into an elegant swan.

This month was also the climax of a period known as the "Lame Duck."

q: Why is February the month of parrots and falcons?
a:
February was associated with love, and what better symbol than the lovebird, itself a small parrot?

Falcons are close relatives of parrots, despite their superficial resemblance to eagles and hawks. In fact, one could think of falcons as murderous parrots -- or parrots as talkative falcons.

q: Why is March the month of crows, ravens, jays, and magpies?
a:
There is ample evidence that March was the month of these intelligent birds.

We know for a fact that March 14 was Pie Day (sometimes spelled Pi Day).

We know for a fact that humans often sang about baking numerous black birds in a pie.

There can be no doubt that magpies were celebrated on Pie Day, and their relatives throughout the month of March.

q: Why is April the month of ostriches, emus, kiwis, and related flightless birds?
a: We have strong evidence that April was a sacred time for Kiwis.

q: How do we know exactly when to celebrate each bird species?
a:
It would have been impossible to know, but Pie Day gave us the key.

Pie Day (sometimes archaically spelled Pi Day) is known to have been celebrated on March 14.

Surely the bird species in question was the yellow-billed magpie, with the scientific name Pica nuttallii.

The "N" in "nuttallii" is the 14th letter of the alphabet, revealing why Pie Day was celebrated on the 14th day of March.

It follows naturally that species beginning with "A" were celebrated on the 1st day of the month, "B" on the 2nd day, etc., and "Z" on the 26th day. 

Species beginning "AA" would be celebrated on the 27th, "AB" on the 28th, etc., through "AE" on the 31st.

The remaining letters of the species name reveal the proper time of day to celebrate.

For example, the "UTTALLII" in "nuttallii" adds up to 21+20+20+1+12+12+9+9 = 104. The tenth hour and the fourth minute, or 10:04.

It's simplicity itself!
